title: Prion-like transmission of human tau strains in the mouse brain.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Fetched the full deposition record for both atomic models from RCSB: 29OS ('AD fold in mouse injected with seeds of AD', cryo-EM, 3.6 Angstrom, 1 polymer entity, 3,300 atoms) and 29OU ('CBD fold in mouse injected with seeds of CBD', 3.4 Angstrom, 2,439 atoms), and downloaded both mmCIF coordinate files (514 KB and 585 KB). Fetched both EMDB (Electron Microscopy Data Bank) map records, EMD-57273 and EMD-57275, each a 192x192x192 voxel density map released 2026-05-27. Checked the bioRxiv preprint (DOI 10.64898/2026.03.30.715211, CC-BY) full text for the data availability statement and its supplementary-material page: the only downloadable supplementary item is the article PDF. Confirmed via paper_context.py that the Nature version is not in PubMed Central and has no supplementary files, no accessions and no NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information) database links indexed.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The counts of human donors (5 Alzheimer's disease cases, 6 corticobasal degeneration cases = 11 brains) and the existence of Supplementary Tables 1-3 (cases, mice used, cryo-EM statistics) come from the bioRxiv full text only; those tables are inside the PDF and were not retrievable as data files. The total number of injected mice is never stated in the retrievable text.

a1_downloadable.note: Passes. Both atomic models and both density maps are freely downloadable with no login; I pulled the mmCIF files myself. The preprint is CC-BY.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Fails. There is no table anywhere in this deposition, so there is no label column. The paper's finding ('the filament grown in mouse has the same fold as the human seed') is a conclusion reached by human structural comparison of two models, not a recorded outcome variable. Any target would have to be constructed from scratch.

a3_inputs_present.note: Passes in a narrow sense: the actual 3D coordinates and density maps are present rather than referenced. But there are only two of each.

a4_units_stated.note: Passes. mmCIF coordinates are in Angstroms and the maps carry voxel size in their headers; these are standard, self-describing formats.

a5_enough_rows.note: Fails catastrophically. The entire deposited dataset is 2 atomic models and 2 density maps, from 11 human brain donors. The checklist floor is ~1,500 labelled rows, or ~400 for classification. Two is three orders of magnitude short.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Passes trivially. Two mmCIF files (~1.1 MB total) and two 192-cubed maps (~28 MB each uncompressed). Fits in memory easily - which is exactly the problem: there is almost nothing there.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Passes. The data availability statement names PDB 29OS/29OU and EMDB 57273/57275; all four exist and their titles match the two experimental arms described.

a8_label_provenance.note: Not a problem in principle. The structures are genuine physical measurements (electron cryo-microscopy of filaments extracted from injected mouse brain), not another model's output. A8 simply never comes into play because there is no label to trace.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available: with two structures there is nothing a model could be trained to say.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use an amyloid filament's three-dimensional shape to predict which brain disease the filament came from.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on three-dimensional structures of tau filaments (tau is a brain protein that clumps into threads in dementia), one example per structure. This paper contributes exactly 2 such structures, verified by opening both coordinate files.
plain_idea.predict: Which disease strain a filament belongs to (Alzheimer's disease fold versus corticobasal degeneration fold). The true answer comes from electron cryo-microscopy, a method that images frozen samples to build an atomic model, performed here by the authors.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Neuropathologists currently assign a tauopathy diagnosis by looking at stained tissue; an automatic structure-to-strain classifier would make the new structure-based disease classification usable at scale. But this paper alone cannot supply the training data.

ml_idea: The only machine-learning idea this paper suggests - classify a tau filament's disease strain from its cryo-EM structure or density map - would need the whole Goedert/Scheres back catalogue of roughly 100-200 deposited tau filament structures pooled from many papers, not this one. Even that pooled set is far below the checklist's row floor and is already solved by eye: an expert assigns the fold in seconds by overlaying backbone traces, so item I4 (is machine learning even the right tool?) would also fail. The genuinely interesting downstream question - what sequence or chemical features make one fold templatable in mouse and another not - is not answerable from two data points.

effort.compute_note: Sizes read directly from the RCSB mmCIF downloads (514 KB and 585 KB) and the EMDB headers (192-cubed voxel grids, ~28 MB each as float32). No timing done because there is no task to time.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the deposited structures named in the data availability statement. It is two. That single count, which took one API call, kills the project.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 and A2 outright. This is a landmark structural biology result - human tau filaments injected into mouse brain regrow with the identical fold, confirming prion-like strain fidelity - but its entire data output is 2 atomic models (PDB 29OS, 29OU) and 2 cryo-EM density maps (EMD-57273, EMD-57275), which I downloaded and inspected. There is no table, no label column and no outcome variable anywhere: the paper's conclusion is a visual comparison of two structures. Two examples cannot train or evaluate anything, and the scientific value here is in the biology, not in any feature/label resource.
